ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Enquiry into Mid-Air Collision of MIG-21 
*41. SHRI SOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA REDDY: Will the Minister of 
DEFENCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether {wo MIG-21 aircrafts collided mid-air and creashed in Assam 
on 16th October, 2000, killing the pilot; 
(b) whether any enquiry has been held to ascertain the causes of this 
collision; 
(c) if so, the details of the Findings in this regard; and 
(d) what steps are being taken to avoid such mishaps in ruture? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES): (a) Yes, 
Sir. 
(b) and (c) Court of Inquiry has been ordered to find the causes for the 
accident and to suggest remedial action, which is still in progress. 
(d) A High Powered Committee on Fighter Aircraft Accidents (COFAA) 
was constituted under the Chairmanship of Scientific Advisor to Raksha Mantri 
to analyse the cause of the accidents, which submitted its report in September, 
1997. It has made certain recommendations to minimise the accident rate. 
Implementation of these recommendations involves changes in organisational 
structure, procedures, training, design, technology etc. About 55 out of 84 
recommendations have since been implemented. 
*Not recorded. 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [22 November, 2000] 
SHRI SOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA REDDY: Mr. Chairman, Sir, it 
is noticed with concern that the number of crashes of the Air Force planes 
has, of late, been increasing. Eighteen crashes have been reported in six 
months. In the recent past, we have lost a large number of costly aircraft in 
accidents. The IAF lost 84 planes in the last five years, causing a loss of 
Rs. 66 crores to the exchequer. We have lost precious lives of pilots. It is 
very unfortunate. 
I feel the maintenance at workshops is not up to the mark or proper 
training of pilots is lacking. This needs to be given proper attention. 
Part (a) of my supplementary to the hon. Minister is: why is the 
induction of defence jet trainers not being expedited to avoid losses? 
Part (b) of my supplementary is: Will the Government assure that the 
aircraft is properly checked after every flight before it takes off. If so, what 
are the proposed guidelines in this regard? 
SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES: Sir, the hon. Member wants to 
know about acquisition of advanced jet trainers. This subject has been 
under discussion for a long period of time. Though the discussion to 
procure one began in 1995, we have been able to find a solution to this 
problem only very recently. The Price Negotiating Committee is currently 
negotiating it. I do hope that by the end of the year, that is, by the end of 
the next month, we will have concluded the formalities in order to procure 
or acquire an advanced jet trainer. 
The hon. Member has also made a point about the upkeep. In so far 
as the upkeep or the maintenance of our aircrft is concerned, there has not 
been any complaint so far. In the various accidents that we have had, pilot 
error or certain defects, technical defects have come to our notice. There 
has not been any case, except one, where the ground maintenance has been 
identified as the cause of the accident. So, Sir, the hon. Member's fear that 
the aircraft maintenance is not being properly done, is not justified. 
SHRI SOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA REDDY: Mr. Chairman, Sir, 
the hon. Minister has stated in his reply that a High-Powered Committee has 
been constituted and it submitted its report in 1997 itself. I want to know 
from the hon. Minister whether the action to implement the remaining 
29 recommendations of the High-Powered Committee would be expedited. 
Have the recommendations involved changes in training pattern, design, 
technology, etc., which are vital for avoiding accidents? By what time the 
recommendations will be implemented fully? 
4 

[22 November, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES: Sir, as I pointed out, the majority 
of the 84 recommendations have been implemented. 
SHRI   SOLIPETA   RAMACH ANDRA   REDDY:   But   
minor recommendations will be very crucial and very important. 
SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES: Sir, the rest are in the process 
of implementation. The delay in their implementation has been 
essentially because of the cost involved in acquiring certain gadgets 
which have been recommended; like simulators, for instance, for each 
variety of aircraft and similar other equipment. They are essentially 
rooted in the availability of resources. In recent times, we have been 
getting additional money to the Defence Ministry from the Budget, and, I 
am sure, Sir, sooner than later, we will complete the implementation of 
these recommendations. 
DR. MANMOHAN SINGH: Mr. Chairman, Sir, it is known that 
during the current year, at least 12 MIG aircraft have crashed. This is a 
very sad state of affairs. The hon. Minister has mentioned about the 
Advanced Jet Trainer. As far as I recall, the decision to acquire the 
Advanced Jet Trainer for the Air Force was taken, as early as in the mid-
nineties. What, then, is the reason that five years have passed and the 
Air Force has still not been supplied with this Advanced Jet Trainer? 
SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES: Sir, as I said, the decision was 
taken in 1995 to acquire, but that decision was not implemented 
because ...(Interruptions)... A decision was taken to acquire, but no 
decision was taken on which aircraft, to acquire at what price, from 
whom to acquire—these decisions have not been taken. The decision 
was an in principle decision. The real exercise to acquire the aircraft 
began only two years back. We have now, for the last one year, a 
committee that is headed by the Vice-Chief of Air Staff which has been 
holding the negotiations, in regard to technical evaluation as well as 
price. So, we have reached the end of an effort that began in 1983. If 
the situation about the MIGs bothers all of us, it is not because there has 
been any lapse on the part of the Government of the day, but it is 
something that we have over a period of time had to put up with. But 
there has been tremendous improvement insofar as... 
SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD: Accidents are concerned. 
SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES: Not at all. The number of 
accidents... (Interruptions)... 
5 

RAJYA SABHA [22 November, 2000] 
SHRI DIPANKAR MUKHERJEE: The Government is a continuing 
entity. Let him explain why this delay has occurred. 
SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES: There has been delay over a period 
of time. ...(Interruptions)... Therefore, our Government has started taking 
steps for acquiring the aircraft. 
SHRI DIPANKAR MUKHERJEE: The Government is a 
continuing entity. We want an explanation as to why this delay has 
occurred. 
SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES: Sir, this is something which began 
in 1983. If we have brought it to fruition today, I would expect the hon. 
Member to appreciate rather than ask me for my explanation. 
SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: Sir, from January to November 
as many as 12 aircraft craches have taken place. There have been reports 
mat many of these have been on account of human error. There have also 
been reports that new pilots are being imparted training on MIG aircraft 
because sophisticated gadgets they are not able to handle that is, the 
immediate response in case of a need, The question for the Minister is, what 
alternatives are being thought of for training these pilots and what shall be 
the time-frame? 
SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES: Sir, human error is something 
about which no one can forecast. What the hon. Member says is true. It is true 
that the majority of these 12 crashes that we have had during the coarse of 
this year, till date, are due to human error and some are due to technical 
defects. And these technical defects are also something that are built into a 
certain situation. An aircraft gets into a spin; there is a flame-out; there is a 
fire; the pilot is unable to retrieve; and you have the problem. But in so far as 
the human error is concerned, Sir, as far as our pilots are concerned, there is no 
doubt whatsoever that they are getting the best training possible and even 
the best can, perhaps, commit an error at a certain point in time. Now, it is 
true that today the MIGs have been described by some as "coffins in the 
air* or "air coffins'...(Interruptions)... Yes, "flying coffins'. Over a period of 
time, the number of accidents has declined. (Interruptions)... 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: No. 
SHRI GHULAM NABI A2AD: That is not true. 
SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES: The number of accidents has gone 
down over the last four decades...(Interruptions)... Four decades ago, the 
average number of accidents used to be around 35- 40 in a year. They came 
down to 30; they came down to 25. Today, they are in the range of 20-25. 
The point I am 
6 

[22 November, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
making is ...(Interruptions)... The point I am making is, over a period of 
time, during the last four decades, there has been a decline in the number of 
accidents. Therefore, when someone today says that the MIG-21 is a 
"flying coffin1, he does not realise that this aircraft has been the mainstay 
for our Air Force. We have the largest number of MIG aircraft in the Air 
Force which includes MIG-21. There is a lot of misinformation about the 
state of affairs. 
SHRI MD. SALIM: Sit, we seek your protection. (Interruptions). 
The question is specific about the MIG accidents. He cannot compare the 
figures of four decades. It is a specific question. (Interruptions)... 
SHRI SURESH KALMADI: Sir, there has been a spate of aircraft 
accidents, especially in the MIG category. I would like to know what the 
life span of the MIG aircraft is and whether you have given extension to it 
and how much extension has been given and how much we are going to 
flog these old aircraft. I also want to know another aspect. It was decided to 
retrofit the MIG aircraft. In this aircraft variety, 125 were supposed to be 
retrofitted. But till today, only two aircraft have been retrofitted In view of 
the ageing of the aircraft, in view of the various accidents which are taking 
place, would you reconsider the decision? Instead of wasting more money 
on retrofit- ting these MiGs, would you consider cancelling it altogether and 
going in for new aircraft? 
SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES: Sir, the MIG aircraft has an average life 
of 35 years. The decision to go in for retrofitting was taken by the Air Force, 
by the Air Headquarters, by those who are flying, those who are in charge 
of the Air Force. When the new Chief took over and he faced the question 
of MiG-21 crashes, he flew the MiG-21 to various stations to demonstrate 
that the MiG-21 is as good an aircraft as any that is there as he pointed out 
once that no aircraft can be declared as not worthy of flying as long as it is 
not certified by the concerned authority as "not fit for flying', and if the 
authority certifies that the aircraft is fit for flying, then it would fly, and that 
is what is happening. Now, the hon. Member wants to know whether we 
will jettison these MIG-21 aircraft and go in for new aircraft. Sir, the hon. 
Member has been in the Air Force. he knows the Air Force better than most 
people in this House, and I am sure, he will accept that if these aircraft still 
have a flying life of ten years or fifteen years, whether they have been 
acquired through subsequent retrofit- ting or by whatever other technical 
exercises, the aircraft will have to fly. Acquisition of new aircraft is a 
process which takes a lot of time, and I am aware thai the Air Force needs to 
be modernised further. We have taken steps in that direction. The Sukois 
are coming, the AGTs are coming, the hawk aircraft have been 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [22 November, 2000] 
identified, and additional squadrons of new aircraft will be necessary, and 
we are in the process of looking at which are the aircraft that may meet our 
actual demand. 
SHRI C. P. THIRUNAVUKKARASU: Sir, the Scientific Advisor 
had advised and submitted a report in September. According to the report, a 
change in design and technololgy has been recommended. The MIG-21 
aircraft was purchased thirty years ago from the U.S.S.R. and the spare 
parts used to be supplied by the U.S.S.R. Now, the U.S.S.R. has totally 
collapsed. I want to know from where you are purchasing the spare parts for 
these aircraft. Are you manufacturing them in India itself or are you 
purchasing them through the public sector undertakings; If the spare parts 
are not good, there will definitely be these sorts of accidents. 
SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES: Sir, there has been indigenization up 
to a point. But where aircraft are concerned, in so far as engines and such other 
basic parts are concerned, we still get those parts from Russia. The U.S.S.R. 
may have collapsed but the Russian Federation exists, and they are the ones 
from whom we are now acquiring whatever we need to acquire. 
DR. KARAN SINGH: Mr. Chairman Sir, by any measure, twelve 
crashes in eleven months is extremely high. I think it is unfair for the 
Minister to go back to forty years and say that the number of crashes in those 
days was more. A At that time, there were oter old fashioned aircraft. But in 
the MIGs themselves, we are losing some of our best and brightest pilots. 
Young men who are trained and who are the cream of our Air Force, we are 
losing them at an alarming rate, and I am sorry to say that the Minister does 
not seem to have given any positive indication in this regard. He is on the 
defensive. He says that we took the decision in 1995. Now five years have 
elapsed for the Advanced Jet Trainers. These bureaucratic procedures, 
prolonged procedures, can gravely compromise our security, because as the 
himself has said that the MIG is the mainstay of our security and our security 
has been gravely endangered in the last few years. Will the Minister give an 
assurance to this House that the Advanced Jet Trainers will be expedited, and 
whatever steps are necessary to make our Air Force effective, will be 
taken. I am sorry to say that the Minister has lost the revolutionary zeal 
and seems to be talkings in purely bureaucratic term. 
SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES: Sir, in March 1998 when I entered 
the Ministry of Defence, there was no aircraft that had been decided to be 
purchased, it was a file, which as I said—and I do not wish to repeat myself 
in the House-that began way back in 1983 and it was still a file which had 
not been decided 
8 

[22 November, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
that a particular aircraft is going to be procured and these are the terms on 
which it is going to be procured. 
DR. KARAN SINGH: You said, 1995. 
SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES: Yes There was a decision. A proposal that 
originated in 1993 reached a certain milestone in 1995. It was in 1998 that I 
dealt with that file and initiated steps. Today we have reached a point where we 
have zeroed in on the aircraft. The technical evaluation is done. It is only the 
price negotiation that remains, and that is partly because we want certain spare 
parts for that aircraft to be made, to meet our requirement and a discussion, 
insofar as those spare parts are concerned, is continuing. We are confident that 
by the end of December, we would have signed the agreement and started the 
process of seeing that those aircraft come.

(a) the details of the news-item published in the Lokmat Samachar 
on the 2nd October, 2000, under the caption, Vridhavastha Pension 
main vridhi hogi; 
(b) whether Government are considering any proposal to provide 
them other facilities also in addition to Vridhavastha pension; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
 
(d) whether Government are also considering the proposal to 
extend concessions to them in the inter- State buses and airlines like 
Air India; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M. 
VENKAIAH NAIDU): (a) to (e) A Statement is laid on the Table of 
the House. 
Statement 
In his Address on the Senior Citizens Day at New Delhi on 1st 
October, 2000 (of which reports a ppeared in the Lokmat Samachar, 
Nagpur, Maharashtra and other newspapers), the Hon'ble Prime 
Minister had, inter alia, observed that while Government has been 
implementing the National Social Assistance Programme for the benefit 
of Senior Citizens who do not have access to economic sustenance and 
the National Old Age Pension Scheme is operated under this 
programme, the amount disbursed under the Scheme being modest, it is 
hoped that it would be possible to in crease the same with the help of 
State Governments. 
In addition to the pensions prov ided by the Central Government 
under the National Old Age Pension component of the National Social 
Assistance Programme, the Government in the Ministry of Rural 
Development have (in April, 2000) launched, the "Annapuma' Scheme 
under which foodgrains @ 10 kgs. per person are provided free of cost 
to aged destitutes, with an approximate coverage of 6.64 lakh persons. 
The care of old persons being primarily the concern of the Ministry of 
Social Justice And Empowerment, that Ministry are implementing An 
Integrated Programme For Older Persons wherein financial assistance 
upto 90% of the project cost is provided to NGOs for the establishment 
and maintenance of Old Age Homes, Day Care Centres and Mobile 
Medical Units as also non- institutional services for older persons. The 
Ministry have a Scheme of Assistance to Panchayati Raj 
Institutions/Voluntary Organisations/ Self-help Groups for the 
construction of Old Age Homes and Mobile Service Centres for older 
persons wherein grant of upto Rs. 30 lakhs is provided to eligible 
persons for, inter alia, the construction of Old Age Homes. 
12 

[22 November, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
The Ministry of Social Justice And Empowerment have indicated 
that they have recently drawn up a National Policy on Older Persons under 
which an Action Plan has been formulated (for the year 2000-2005) 
which is to be implemented in conjunction with various Ministries / 
Departments. As per this Action Plan, the Ministries of Surface Transport 
and Civil Aviation would consider:- 
(i) Fare concessions to senior citizens in Buses. 
(ii) Design buses to provide for easy entrance, exit and safety. 
(iii) Reservation of seats for older persons in Buses. 
(iv) Whether facilities could be provided to senior citizens to make 
air travel a comfortable experience and to lower the age of 
entitlement for air fare concessions for women. 
Amongst the other initiatives reported to have been taken by the 
Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment in pursuance of the National 
Policy on Older persons are:—  
(i) The National Council for Older Persons (NCOP) has been set 
up on 10th May, 1999 to operationalize the Policy. The first 
meeting of NCOP was held at New Delhi on 13th June, 2000. 
The members discussed the draft Action Plan for 
implementation of the National Policy on Older Persons. The 
process of finalisation of Action Plan is in progress. 
(ii) Aadhar has been set up to function as Secretariat of NCOP. It is 
being administered by Agewell Foundation, an NGO, with the 
financial assistance from the Ministry. The ma jor activities 
of Aadhar include receiving and taking follow up action on 
representations, the complaints and grievances of older 
persons. 
(iii) Both the ongoing Schemes of  the Ministry for Welfare of 
Older Persons have been reviewed and revised in the light of the 
National Policy. 
(iv) The Ministry commissioned a project called OASIS (an 
acronym for Old Age Social and Income Security) and 
appointed an 8 member Expert Committee, headed by Dr. S. 
A. Dave, former Chairman of UTI, to examine policy questions 
connected with old age income security in India and submit its 
recommendations to the Government. The Committee 
submitted its final report on 11.1.2000.

expeditions disposal of Court Cases involving Older Persons. 
(vi) The Union Health Ministry has issued instructions to all the State 
Governments / UT Administrations for provision of separate queues 
for older persons at all stages. 
(vii) At the initiative and with the financial assistance of this Ministry, 
a Telephone Helpline for older Persons has been made functional 
from April, 1999 by an NGO called Agewell Foundation. 
(viii) The National Institute of Social Defence has started a six months 
course for home care of elderly disabled persons. This course will 
help to prepare a cadre of Geriatric Animators to render 
comprehensive care to the aged in their homes and in the 
community.

sophisticated weapons and communication system etc.

with regard to implementing effective border management. The concerned

India and Nepal, to counter activities inimical to India's interests.

Monitoring of Dispatched Ammunition 
260. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of DEFENCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that recently a wagon load of high calibre 
ammunition dispatched by the Ordnance Depot at Jabalpur to the 
Naval Armament Depot, Uran, was found lying undetected for over 
two years in a derelict railway yard near Bhayandar, a North Mumbai 
suburb; 
(b) if so, the reasons for keeping quiet for two years on the 
dispatched dangerous ammunition and allowing it to slip into a 
neglected railway yard; and 
(c) whether the existing guidelines to monitor the ammunition 
dispatched through the Railways are considered adequate and are 
being followed? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE 
FERNANDES): (a) to (c) A wagon loaded with high caliber ammunition 
was despatched by Ordnance Factory, Khamaria at Jabalpur to NAD 
Karanja on 1-12-1997 vide Railway Receipt No. D 111511 dated 1-12-
1997. The despatch details along with the Railway receipt was sent by 
Ordnance Factory, Khamaria to the consignee who was to monitor 
recept of the consignment. NAD, Ka ranja took up the issue of non-
receipt of the consignment with the Chief Commercial Superintendent, 
Central Railway, CST, Mumbai by letter dated 18-5-1998 endorsing 
copy to Ordnance Factory, Khamaria. On receipt of information, 
Ordnance Factory Khamaria also took up the matter with appropriate 
Railway authorities and detailed personnel to various probable stations 
en-route as also to stations as far as Mysore and Chennai where it 
could have been mistakenly diverted to locate the consignment. A 
continuous effort was made by Ordnance Factory, Khamaria to trace 
the wagon in consultation with ra ilway authorities. The wagon in 
question was finally received at NAD, Karanja on 7-9-2000. 
Immediately after despatch of a consignment, the consignor 
intimates the despatch details to the consignee to monitor the receipt of 
the consignment on regular basis. Non-receipt of consignment within 
reasonable time is brought to the notice of the consignor and a joint 
effort is made both by consignee and consignor to trace the wagon. In 
addition necessary action through law and

RAJYA SABHA [22 November, 2000] 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES): (a) 
to (c) Kaya La is a common Watershed Pass located on the India-China 
LAC in Dibang valley of Arunachal Pradesh. The Chinese have 
constructed a mule track in their territory upto the Pass. While it is difficult 
to define the centre of a Pass due to its width, the said track is apparently 
extended to our side of the Pass by about 50 metres. A protest has been 
lodged with the Chinese. 
The resolution of the boundary question between India and China is 
outstanding. The two sides have also differences in the perception of the 
Line of Actual Control (LAC) in the border areas. Both sides carry out 
patrolling activity as per their respective perception of the LAC. Violations 
of the LAC are taken up through diplomatic channels and Border 
Personnel Meetings/ Flag meetings. The situation along the India-China 
border has remained generally peaceful and under control. 
India and China have been discussing the boundary question in the 
framework of the Joint Working Group. Both sides have reiterated the 
objective of seeking a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable settlement of 
the boundary question through dialogue. Nevertheless, Government 
remain vigilant and take all nece ssary and appropriate measures to 
safeguard the sovereignty, territorial integrity and security of India.

Safety and security of common people 
293. PROF. M.M. AGARWAL: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the details of effective measures being taken by Government to provide 
adequate safety and security to the common people in the country; 
(b) whether it is a fact that Government have failed to provide adequate 
safety and security to the people of Bihar, Jammu and Kashmir, NER belt and 
other backward districts of the country; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI CHENNAMANENI VIDYA SAGAR RAO): (a) to (c) Despite some areas 
of concern, the law and order situation in the country is under control. The 
major concerns centre around Pak-sponsored terrorism in Jammu & Kashmir, 
inter-linked and externally supported subversive activities of militant groups 
in the North-East and the violence perpetrated by the Left Wing Extremist 
groups. "Public Order" and "Police" are State subjects and maintenance of law 
and order is the primary responsibility of the State Governments. It is for the 
State Governments to devise various methods and take concrete steps to improve 
the law and order situation in their States. The Central Government, however, 
keeps a close watch on various developments in the internal security scenario 
of the country and sensitises the concerned States in this regard. It also shares 
intelligence with the States from time to time. Central Para-Military Forces are 
also deployed whenever required by the States. Funds are also provided under 
various schemes to modernise and strenthen the State Police Forces.

Statement 
Pending Border Disputes between Different States 
Maharashtra-Karnataka border dispute: 
Eversince the Reorganisaiton of states in 1956, there has been 
boundary dispute between Maharahstra and Karnataka, both 
demanding re-adjustment of boundaries on the basis of the language 
spoken by the people of their area. 
103 

RAJYA SABHA [22 November, 2000] 
Earlier efforts to resolve the dispute through mutual agreement having failed, 
theCbvemment of India appointed the Mahajan Commission in October, 1966. 
The Commission submitted its report on 2S.8.1967. Out of the total of 814 
villages claimed by State of Maharahstra, the Commission had recommended 
that 264 villages along with the towns of Nipani, Khanapur and Nandgad may 
be transferred from Karnataka to Maharashtra. The claim of Maharashtra to the 
town of Belgaum was rejected. Out of 260 villages claimed by Karnataka, the 
Commission recommended transfer of 227 villages to Karnataka from 
Maharashtra. While the Government  of Karnataka insisted on the 
implementation of the recommendations of die Mahajan Commission in toto, 
the Government of Maharashtra did not accept the recommendations. The 
dispute, therefore, continues to exist. 
Orissa-Andhra Pradesh border dispute: 
The boundary disputes between Orissa and Andhra pradesh relates to 63 
villages. Disputes relating to Kotiya group of 21 villages and Borramutha 
(total 22 villages) of Koraput district in Orissa dates back to 19SS and the 
dispute relating to rest 41 villages with Andhra Pradesh dates back to 1981-82. 
Punjab-Haryana-Himachal Pradesh border dispute: 
Consequent upon the reorganisation of the composite Punjab State in 
1966, the Central Government announced its decision on these disputes in 
1970. This included transfer of Chandigarh to Punjab and part of FazilkaTehsil 
of Punjab to Haryana etc. Three Commissions have been appointed so far to 
determine the specific Hindi speaking areas of Punjab which should go to 
Haryana in lieu of Chandigarh. 
Uttar Pradesh-Bihar and Uttar Pradesh-Haryana border dispute: 
The deep stream of river Ganga and Yamuna formed inter-State boundary 
between some parts of Uttar Prades h-Bihar and Haryana-Uttar Pradesh 
respectively. Due to frequent changes in the course of the river, the inter-state 
boundary keeps on fluctuating. Due to this disputes persist.

pleased

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) While most of the States have 
evinced interest in undertaking power sector reforms, the States of Orissa, 
Haryana, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Delhi, Madhya 
Pradesh and Gujarat have taken discernible progress towards reforms. 
(b) The broad features of me reforms programme are—Enactment of 
the Reforms Bill, constitution/operationalisation of State Electricity 
Regulatory 
113 

RAJYA SABHA [22 November, 2000] 
Commissions, to bring in the elements of accountability in the SEBs, 
improvement of Transmission & Distribution systems and distribution 
reforms. 
(c) States of Orissa, Haryana, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh 
and Rajasthan have enacted their Reforms Acts. State of Delhi has 
promulgated Reforms Ordinance. Government of Madhya Pradesh has drafted 
Reforms Bills which is being introduced in the Assembly. Government of 
Gujarat has also drafted Reforms Bill and forwarded it for approval of 
Government of India before introducing in the State Assembly. 
SEBs of Orissa, Haryana, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh and 
Rajasthan have been unbundled. Delhi Vidyut Board is proposed to be 
unbundled within 3 months. 
States of Orissa, Haryana, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh, West 
Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Punjab, Delhi, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Arunachal 
Pradesh, Maharashtra and Rajasthan have constituted/notified their State 
Electricity Regulatory Commissions (SERCs). SERCs of Orissa, Andhra 
Pradesh, Maharashtra, UP and Gujarat have already issued tariff orders. 
Distribution in Orissa has been fully privatised. BSES Ltd. has taken 
over the three distribution companies (WESCO, NORTHCO & SOUTHCO) 
and the US based AES Ltd. has take n over the Central Zone (CESCO). 
Though the overall financial position of the GRIDCO has not shown 
improvement, the private distribution'companies have shown improved 
collection of revenue on an average by 20% over a period of one year. The 
collection performance in Low Tension (LT) sector has shown 
improvement. This is despite the fact that Orissa was hit by worst ever 
eyelone immediately after privatisation.

privatise distribution by year 2001- 2002.

consumers by December, 2001. 
(iii)   Reduction and finally elimination of power theft within

distribution system by taking sub-station as an unit on a

penetration and maintain a dominant presence in the

segments of the textile industry are enabled to perform in

ALLEVIATION (SHRI JAGMOHAN): Hon. Chairman, Sir, On 
14.11.2000 the Supreme Court issued the following orders: 
"In the first instance, we, therefore, issue notice to the 
Chief Secretary, Delhi and also to the Commissioner, 
MCD to show cause why they should not be punished 
for contempt for the continued inaction on the part of 
.the NCT, Delhi and for the noncompliance of the 
various orders passed by this Court starting from 1996 
and including the orders dated 08.09.1999, 30.08.2000 
and 12.09.2000 regarding the closing of the polluting 
units situated in the residential areas." 
Thereafter, the officials of the Government of National 
Capital Territory of Delhi and Municipal Corporation started 
sealing polluting as well as other industries in residential areas. 
This led to unrest involving road blocks leading to traffic jams, 
burning of buses, etc. To facilitate understanding of the present 
position, it is necessary to recount the developments that have 
taken place from February 02, 1996, that is the date from which 
the Court started passing orders regarding closure/relocation of 
industries from the residential ar eas. The order of February 02, 
1996 reads: 
"Learned counsel agree that a High Power Committee 
be constituted which can examine as to which type of 
industries can be permitted in a residential area. We. 
therefore, direct the Chief Secretary, NCT, Delhi, to 
constitute a Committee consisting of one Member each 
from NCT, Delhi, Central Pollution Control Board, Delhi 
Pollution Control Committee, Municipal Corporation, 
Delhi, and Delhi Electric Supply Undertaking (DESU). 
The Chairman of the Committee shall be representative 
of NCT, Delhi Administration. The Committee shall be 
constituted by the Chief Secretary, NCT, Delhi 
Administration within two weeks of the receipt of this 
order by the Chief Secretary." 
On 04-10-1996, the Court noted that the then Principal 
Secretary to the Government of National Capital Territory of 
Delhi had filed an affidavit intimating the progress of the High 
Powered Committee set up by the Court. It was stated that out 
of 45,000 applications received, after deleting the duplicate 
applications, 43,045 applications were scrutinised. Of these, 
39,166 applications did not qualify for grant of necessary 
permission under 
168 

[22 November, 2000]      RAJYA SABHA 
the Master Plan. The remaining 3,879 units/applications were 
inspected by a Committee constituted of MCD, Department of 
Industries, Delhi Electric Supply Undertaking and Delhi 
Pollution Control Committee. This Committee found only 376 
units to qualify for grant of permission to run the units in the 
residential area. 
On December 18, 1996, the then Principal Secretary to 
Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi assured the 
Court, through an affidavit filed on December 18, 1996, that 
possession of 1,300 acres would be taken by the NCT and 
forms for allotments were being supplied to the industries.   In 
its order of December 18, 1996, the Court observed: 
"We reiterate that we are satisfied that the NCT, Delhi 
Administration is seriously processing the project of 
relocating the industries operating in residential/non-
conforming areas of Delhi. We are further satisfied that 
the Industries are also co-operating...It has taken quite 
some time for the Delhi Administration to realise the 
importance of the matter and to get into the grip of the 
matter. The Government having now taken up the 
matter seriously, it is time for this Court to step aside as 
at present and leave the field for the Government to act 
on its own and relocate the industries in accordance with 
the plan formulated by this Court...The NCT. Delhi 
Administration shall file progress report in this Court 
every three months." 
Subsequently, however, since the Court noted no 
progress, it had started making adverse comments on non-
compliance of its orders. 
The present situation has arisen due to failure of the 
Government of National Territory of Delhi to develop plots for 
relocation of industries in Bawana and other areas. In this 
connection, it needs to be underlined that the Supreme Court 
started passing orders from February 02, 1996, and up till 
December 09, 1999, no one talked of amending the Master 
Plan. 
The Government are aware of the problems that are 
being faced by the industries functioning in the residential 
areas as well as of the house-owners and occupiers who are 
using their property for residentia l purposes in the residential 
areas. The Government are keen to find a solution which would 
be just and fair to all concerned. The Government have agreed, 
in principle, subject to observance of safeguards in respect of 
169 

RAJYA SABHA    [22 November, 2000] 
pollution norms, to redefine household industries in terms of the 
recommendations made by a Committee, known as the Jagdish 
Sagar Committee. These norms pertain to the number of 
persons who can work in household industries, the power that 
can be sanctioned and the area that can be used, etc. 
The Government would also amend the Master Plan, if 
necessary, to acquire more land for relocation of industries in 
industrial areas. 
The Government would also request the Supreme Court 
to give a little more time for relocation. The matter at present 
rests with the Supreme Court. (Interruptions) [Placed in Library.

Shifting of Industries from Residential Areas of Delhi. 
DR. KARAN SINGH (Delhi): Mr, Chairman, Sir, the 
events that have taken place in Delhi over the last three days 
have been of a tremendous magnitude. The whole of Delhi is in 
turmoil; lakhs of people are on the roads, there has been a 
breakdown of law and order; people have died; dozens have 
been injured; and the whole of the beautiful capital is in 
absolute turmoil,   and tarnished. 
Sir, at a moment like this, we had expected that instead 
of trying to place blame upon one party or the other, the 
Government would come forward with some constructive 
proposal to meet the requirement. But what has happened? In 
fact, in his statement, the Minister has tried to place the blame 
upon the Delhi Government. Let me point out to you, Sir, that in 
1996, when the Supreme Court first opined upon this, it was the 
B.J.P. Government which was in power. They were the ones 
which were in power in 1996, 1997 and 1998. For three years, 
they were in power, and they did not take any adequate steps 
to meet this problem. It is only after the Congress Government 
came to power that we began seriously the processes of 
acquisition of land, and of trying to develop it. Sir, the basic 
point which I would- like to make is that without an amendment 
to the Master Plan, it is not possible to solve this problem. I 
would like the House to be very clear on this, and that is the 
one point where the hon. Minister has been extremely stubborn, 
if I may say so. He says that the question was not raised about 
the Master Plan. Will the Minist er clarify, whether or not, the 
present Chief Minister of Delhi has on more than one occasion 
met with the Minister personally, and pleaded with him to 
change the Master Plan without which the problem cannot be 
solved? But instead of doing that, he rejected this out of hand. 
He said that there is no question of changing the Master Plan. 
We have seen him say that on television. 
Sir, if the Constitution can be amended 85 times, surely 
the Master Plan is not something which cannot be touched. 
Certainly, we want a pollution-free Delhi. I have been a 
conservationist all my life. We have talked about conservation, 
but this is a human problem. There are lakhs of people whose 
daily life is disrupted, and if this is carried through, there will be 
a total turmoil and chaos in Delhi. Now, at last, I am afraid, this 
is becoming a pattern of this Government.    They hold on 
stubbornly till the 
174 

[22 November, 2000]      RAJYA SABHA 
end, and then under pressure, they collapse. They did the 
same thing with the oil prices. Now, at last, today, for the first 
time, the hon. Minister has said that they are prepared to 
amend the Master Plan. If he had said this earlier, if he had 
said this two years ago when it was first mooted, this problem 
would not have been very serious. Let me make it very clear 
that this is a problem which can be solved only with the full 
cooperation of the Ministry of Urban Development, of the Delhi 
Government, of the M.C.D., and with the cooperation of all the

plots have been allotted in the industrial areas of Narela, 
Jhilmil, Patparganj, Badli, Bawana. They need to be developed.

infrastructure in order to develop them. What we have to do is 
to amend the Master Plan so that those industries, which are 
particularly the non-polluting industries, should be allowed to 
stay where they are.

industrial concentration have got to be declared industrial 
areas. Thirty years' development has taken place in Delhi.

over one-and-a-half crores of people who live in the Capital 
Region area. It is not only the people in posh colonies who live 
here, it is also those people who live in those areas. I agree 
that pollution hits them the worst. But it has to be done in a 
humanitarian, humane and imaginative manner. This sort of 
rigid attitude that the Government took which resulted in this 
fiasco has created the absolute havoc.

RAJYA SABHA    [22 November, 2000] 
It is very clear that the Delhi Government has tried its 
best to persuade the Ministry of Urban Development to change 
the Master Plan, but they have not agreed to do so, as a result 
of which this crisis has arisen today. I do not want to get into 
party polemics. I think it is unfair for the Minister to try to blame 
the present Government that has been in power only for less 
than two years, whereas there were three Chief Ministers of the 
BJP in the previous administration. 
My other colleagues are going to talk in more detail 
about the problems actually being faced.   I want to make three 
points: 
One, this is a massive problem, involving tens of lakhs 
of people, millions of people. It is something that has to be dealt 
with immediately. Otherwise, the law and order situation in 
Delhi will collapse, and it will spin out of control. We know what 
happens when the law and order situation collapses in the 
capital. This is not only the capital of those who live in Delhi or 
who represent Delhi, but it is the capital of every Indian. 
Therefore, we cannot allow this capital to be destroyed in this 
manner So, immediate steps must be taken. 
I would also appeal to the people who are involved, who 
are deeply disturbed and who are deeply distressed, from the 
Chief Minister down to common citizens. I would plead with 
them to show a little tolerance, to wait for a while, not to resort 
to violence and to try to see that this problem is solved. 
Two, it is not enough to say that the Government would 
amend the Master Plan also, if necessary, to acquire more 
land. The Government has got to amend the Master Plan. That 
must take place immediately. It is not just something that can 
be done in future because, unless the Master Plan is amended, 
there is no way in which this problem can be solved. 
Three, Sir, I would suggest that the Urban Development 
Ministry, the Delhi Administration, all the concerned authorities 
and all the citizens of Delhi, the civil society, should get 
together at this juncture and prevent the city from being 
destroyed. We must make a plea to the Supreme Court that 
whatever might have happened in the past, there is now a 
determination to solve this problem. The citizens of Delhi must 
be involved in the antipollution drive and school children have 
got to be involved, students have to be involved.   We have to 
create a climate of opinion to make Delhi a 
176 

[22 November, 2000]     RAJYA SABHA 
clean city. You may remember that 20 years ago I was the 
Chairman of the Joint Committee that looked into the provisions 
of the Air Pollution Act. We went around the Taj also. I will bring 
it up separately. Hon. Members might have read my statement 
that the Taj is beginning to change its colour. About Delhi, we 
talked about the Badarpur Refinery. We talked about all the 
major pollutants that do not belong to individuals but to the 
Government.  There has to be a coordinated drive. 
It is no use, Mr. Minister, trying to pass the buck or 
trying to blame the Delhi Administration. Your own MPs from 
Delhi itself have been unhappy about your rigidity with regard 
to the Master Plan. They have gone to you and they have gone 
to the Prime Minister to urge that the Master Plan should be 
amended. 
So, Sir, my plea in this is, we are facing a crisis 
situation. We have got to deal with it in a humane, matured and 
mutually co-operative manner. I hope the Minister, instead of 
indulging in party polemics, will rise above that and try and see 
that the problems of millions of people in Delhi are solved. 
Thank you.

SHRI R. MARGABANDU (Tamil Nadu): Madam, the 
Order of the Supreme Court is dated 2 nd February 1996, by 
which the High Powered Committee was constituted for the 
purpose of examining as to which type of industries can be 
permitted in the residential areas. So, the job assigned to the 
High Powered Committee was to find out the nature of 
industries, i.e., polluting and non-polluting, and the non-
polluting industries can be permitted to operate in the 
residential areas, whereas the polluting industries can be 
housed in a different place. Madam, the statement of the 
Minister does not indicate the number of polluting industries, 
and what steps have been taken to relocate them at other 
places. I want to know whether any other place has been 
identified for relocating them. If so, how many industries have 
been relocated so far? That is wanting in the statement. 
Madam, there are two components involved in this 
issue. One is the industry-owners and workers; and the other is 
the common people who are affected by health hazards. These 
are the two divergent groups whose interests have to be 
reconciled. For healthy living of the people, action has to be 
taken by the Government, without shifting the responsibility 
between the previous Government and the present 
Government. It is a problem concerning the common people. 
The Supreme Court in its order said that in the case of polluting 
industries, they should be located away from the residential 
areas and they should be housed in a separate industrial place. 
The statement of the Minister does not indicate What steps 
have so far been taken in this direction. It is also not made 
clear in the statement as to what defence or position has been 
taken before the Supreme Court and how much time they want, 
to relocate these industries. So, all these things are wanting in 
the statement.

Madam, as per a report, there are 97,600 industrial 
units in Delhi. Out of this, how many industries are non-
polluting? The statement does not contain such details. As per 
newspaper reports, about 167 industries have been demolished 
and about 20,000 people have been thrown into the streets. 
They are suffering" a lot as they are not getting the minimum 
amenities which are necessary for a decent living. While taking 
action, no doubt, the Delhi Government is facing contempt 
proceedings before the Supreme Court, as it has to obey and 
carry out the orders of the Supreme Court. Before carrying out 
the orders of the Supreme Court, they should have taken steps 
to see that the employees and the workers are given proper 
compensation, alternate accommodation, etc. But no such thing 
has been given to them. The report says that many of the 
labourers have gone to the labour court, as they were suffering 
a lot, because no alternative arrangement had been made for 
their jobs, etc. 
The industrial owners have not come forward to 
safeguard the interests of the industrial workers. It is also cited, 
Madam, that the industries ar e housed in small houses where 
there is no ventilation, where there is no sufficient place to 
work. It is also reported that 50 people have died in the places 
of work itself, for want of a healthy environment. So, these 
things will have to be taken into account. The Government 
should not be hasty in demolishing it. At the same time, the 
Government has got the responsibility to safeguard the health 
of the common people. Towards this end, steps should be 
taken. There is a need for reconciling these two ideologies. 
There should be a balanced approach to relocate the units, 
without affecting the health of the common people. 
As a matter of fact, in several High Courts, including the 
Chennai High Court, there is a Green Bench, which is 
constituted in order to deal with cases relating to pollution. 
There are cases where the orders of the High Court and the 
Supreme Court are not complied with by the industries. As a 
result, pollution is affecting the entire people. In order to 
safeguard the humanity, the pollution must be brought under 
control. 
With these words, I conclude.

being displaced either due to natural calamities or due to man-
made disasters. Whether it is the case of people affected by 
the closure of polluting units; whether it is the case of people 
dispiaced by the Narmada Dam; or whether it is the case of 3 
lakh p.eople being asked to vacate the Sanjay Gandhi National 
Park in Bombay; the court goes ahead and issues its directives, 
The Government, in turn, drags its feet and simply says, "We 
do not have the land. What shall we do?" What action is taken 
against these Governments when they fail to provide the 
compensation that the court says they must give 7    The Court 
just gives its directive; the Government throws its hands 
218 

[22 November, 2000]      RAJYA SABHA 
4.00 P.M 
back. What will happen to the people? There is a situation at 
the moment in the Sanjay Gandhi National Park, where the 
Maharashtra Government is sitting on 10 crores of rupees, 
which has been taken from the people, by the Government for 
the Sanjay Gandhi National Park. For an alternative 
accommodation, they gave Rs. 7,000/- each. Today, they are 
facing the bulldozers because no alternative accommodation is 
provided to them. They have giv en the money, but all they are 
faced with is demolition. So, the kind of signal that we give is, 
there are two types of laws in this country. There is a separate 
law for the rich, and there is a separate law for the poor We 
have instances without number that when it comes to the rich 
and when they routinely violate laws, they are never in fear of 
being evicted They are never in fear of their houses being 
demolished. In fact, they are protected. The question of 
adhering to the law comes only when it comes to the poor and 
the marginalized people of this country. 
The statement of the Minister, after carefully 
apportioning all the blame on the Delhi Government, 
conveniently forgetting its own role when it was in power in 
Delhi and did nothing to solve the problem, now says that the 
Government would amend the Master Plan, if necessary. Is 
there any doubt that the Master Plan needs to be amended? In 
fact, why has it not been amended till now? What is so 
sacrosanct about the Master Plan? The Master Plan has 
routinely been changed, why can't it be altered in this particular 
situation as well? We have to take into account new ground 
realities. 
However, I would again like to emphasise that this case 
cannot be seen in isolation. We need to realise that it is the 
absence of a clearly defined rehabilitation policy that is 
responsible for this sorry state of affairs. When the repeal of the 
Urban Land Ceiling Act, which was initiated by this 
Government, was being discussed, it were NGOs and activists 
who shouted themselves hoarse that repealing this Act would 
really be throwing the baby out with the bath water because 
land is a very important resource in the hands of the 
Government and should not be given away to the rich; because 
no Government is going to buy land at market rates to 
rehabilitate the poor and the displaced. It gives me no joy to 
say this; in fact, what we were saying is being proved true 
every single day. 
219 

RAJYA SABHA    [22 November, 2000] 
The real malaise goes far deeper than the Master Plan 
or relocating the polluting industries. The violent reaction seen 
on the streets of Delhi is the inevitable spin off from populist 
policies and demagoguery. The authorities look the other way 
when urban laws are violated. Where were they when the 
same units against whom action is being taken now were 
coming up? By what logic can tailoring units and garages be 
put in the same bracket as plants without effluent treatment 
units, irrespective of where they are located. 
Anti-people policies, short-term solutions, adherence to 
the law, comes only when the poor and the marginalised are 
affected. This is not the way justice is done. It is all very well for 
the Government to say that it seeks more time from the 
Supreme Court. • What does the Government intend to do with 
this more time, I would like to know. 
Concluding this, I would say that while this is a question 
which cannot and should not be treated as an adversarial one, it is 
a question which has to be resolved, not on the basis of past 
mistakes or who made them, but by doing something so as to 
help the poor people to survive. The question whether the right 
to pollution- free air should be preferred to right to livelihood, 
depends on who is asked the question. A person living in 
luxury would say 'pollution-free air is of paramount importance.' 
A person living in poverty would say 'the right to livelihood is of 
paramount importance.' If a person living from hand to mouth is 
asked whether he would prefer to die at 50, in pollution-ridden 
air or he would prefer to live without any means of livelihood in 
pollution free air, till the age of 60, there is no doubt in my mind 
what he would choose. 
If alleviation of human misery can be achieved by paying 
regard to environment, that would be ideal. But if alleviation of 
human misery cannot be achieved whilst, sustaining the 
environment simultaneously, then, I am afraid the former would 
be of paramount importance. We will have to live with a little 
more pollution a little while longer, till we are able to ensure 
both aspects, that is, right to life guaranteed by article 21 - the 
right to livelihood - and the right to a healthy environment.  Thank 
you.
